planting.note: Mount or pot in a chunky, fast-draining epiphyte mix (bark, perlite, sphagnum) and grow in a hanging basket or on a slab in bright, filtered light; let the mix dry between waterings and provide extra humidity to keep the leaf coloring vivid.

directions: Hoya sigillatis is a slender, trailing epiphytic vine endemic to Borneo, distinguished by olive-green leaves overlaid with an irregular silvery-white splash pattern above and a burgundy-maroon reverse that deepens in stronger light. Unlike the smooth or heavily veined leaves of other Hoyas in this dataset, sigillatis foliage has a soft, slightly puckered texture and a two-toned front-and-back contrast that makes it a favorite among collectors even outside of bloom. Flat-faced umbels of up to 20 small caramel-orange flowers open along the trailing stems and release a strong, sweet fragrance often compared to caramel or brown sugar. Best grown in a basket where the thin stems can cascade freely; it resents overly wet, cold mix far more than it resents dry spells.
sources: Steve's Leaves — Hoya sigillatis species profile
Vermont Hoyas — Hoya sigillatis cultivation notes
Kew Plants of the World Online — Hoya sigillatis

planting.note: Grow in a hanging basket or on a small trellis in bright, filtered light; strong (but indirect) light intensifies the red leaf blush that gives this species its appeal, while low light keeps leaves plain green and the vine leggy.

directions: Hoya waymaniae is a Bornean species grown chiefly for its thick, oval leaves, which flush a deep brick-red across the leaf blade in bright light while the veins stay contrastingly green, giving the foliage a stained-glass appearance unlike any other Hoya in this collection. Clusters of small, star-shaped flowers in warm orange or yellow tones, each centered with a red or purple corona, open along the vine and carry a sweet, honeyed fragrance rather than the spicier or muskier scents typical of other species here. Growth is a modest twining vine, well suited to a small hanging pot or trellised windowsill spot rather than a large trained specimen. Allow the mix to dry between waterings; waterlogging is the most common cause of leaf drop.
sources: Logee's Plants — Hoya waymaniae
Steve's Leaves — Hoya waymaniae species profile
Vermont Hoyas — Hoya waymaniae (IML 1756)

planting.note: Provide a sturdy trellis or wall support and grow in bright, filtered light with warm temperatures; this is a vigorous climber that needs several feet of mature vine before it will flower, so patience and a permanent support are essential.

directions: Hoya lauterbachii, native to Papua New Guinea, is grown for producing some of the largest flowers in the entire genus — umbels of up to eight reddish-copper, cream-centered blooms that can each approach the width of a saucer, covered in fine hairs and releasing a rich, chocolate-like fragrance. The velvety, softly fuzzy leaves carry faint silver accents over deep green, a texture distinct from the glossy or waxy foliage of most other Hoyas in this dataset. Unlike compact species such as Hoya curtisii or serpens, lauterbachii is a robust, vigorous climber that needs six to eight feet of vine and a real support structure before it reaches flowering maturity. Give it warm temperatures, bright filtered light, and a loose, chunky mix that dries out between thorough waterings.
sources: Logee's Plants — Giant Wax Plant (Hoya lauterbachii)
Hoya Store Australia — Hoya lauterbachii
plantlust — Eriostemma lauterbachii (Hoya lauterbachii)

planting.note: Grow in a small hanging pot in bright, indirect light with a well-draining bark-and-perlite mix; native to shaded Thai rainforest understory, this species wants higher humidity than most houseplant Hoyas and resents cold, wet roots.

directions: Hoya subquintuplinervis, native to the rainforest understory of northern Thailand and surrounding Southeast Asia, is grown for its thick, oval, succulent-textured leaves, which show a network of pale, prominently raised veins against a darker green blade — a strongly patterned look distinct from the smooth foliage of species like Hoya obovata or the pitted texture of lacunosa. It produces small clusters of pure white, star-shaped flowers without the pink or red coronas seen in most other Hoya flowers, giving it a cleaner, more understated bloom. The plant stays compact and slow-growing compared to the genus's larger vines, making it well suited to a small hanging pot on a shelf or windowsill. Keep humidity elevated and let the mix dry between waterings to avoid root rot.
sources: Unsolicited Plant Talks — Hoya subquintuplinervis species notes
Hoya Plants — Hoya subquintuplinervis
greg.app — Hoya subquintuplinervis care overview

planting.note: Grow on a small trellis or as a trailing basket plant in bright, filtered light; this root-climbing species will cling to bark or moss poles given the chance, or trail attractively if left unsupported.

directions: Hoya pottsii is a slender, root-climbing vine with pointed, dark-green leaves crossed by conspicuously raised veins that give the foliage a corrugated, ridged surface — a rougher texture than the smooth leaves of related species such as Hoya bilobata. Its flowers open in compact, umbrella-shaped clusters of small white-to-cream, waxy stars, and although the scent is milder than that of Hoya lacunosa, the blooms release a pleasant fragrance most noticeable after dark. Growth habit is a slim twining-and-root-clinging vine that will attach itself to rough bark or moss if given a pole to climb, or can simply be left to trail from a basket. Provide bright filtered light and let the mix dry between waterings for the best flowering.
sources: Steve's Leaves — Hoya pottsii species profile
Lucid Central — Hoya pottsii (rainforest key entities)
Chinese Academy of Sciences — pollinator research on Hoya pottsii

planting.note: Grow on a small trellis or moss pole in bright, filtered light; the woody-based twining stems benefit from support once mature, and blooms are longest-lasting (7-10 days per cluster) when the plant is not moved during flowering.

directions: Hoya buotii, named for Philippine botanist Inocencio Buot Jr., is a twining vine with a woody base and light-green, elliptical leaves whose margins and pointed tips curl noticeably downward, a leaf silhouette that sets it apart from the flatter foliage of Hoya bilobata or imperialis. Its fragrant flower clusters, up to about 3 cm across, open in dense heads on short stalks and are among the more visually complex in the genus: pale to dull yellow, densely hairy corolla lobes are sometimes washed with violet, surrounding a cream-to-white corona that flushes red toward the center. Blooms appear in spring and summer and last roughly a week to ten days per flush, a comparatively long display. The plant is a manageable twining vine, easily grown up a small trellis or moss pole in a bright, humid spot.
sources: World of Succulents — Hoya buotii
NParks Singapore FloraFaunaWeb — Hoya buotii Kloppenb.
Steve's Leaves — Hoya buotii

planting.note: Grow in a hanging basket or trellised pot in bright, filtered light; leaves develop a protective red flush in strong light, so gradually acclimate plants moved from low-light interiors before giving them full bright exposure.

directions: Hoya nicholsoniae ranges naturally across New Caledonia, New Guinea, coastal Queensland, Samoa, and the Solomon Islands, a broader South Pacific distribution than most Hoyas in this dataset. Its small, pointed leaves are threaded with prominent veins and redden noticeably as a light-protective response when grown in strong, bright conditions. Rounded umbels of 20-30 creamy-yellow flowers open at once and give off a distinctly spicy fragrance, quite different from the caramel or cinnamon notes of other species here, with each flush lasting around four to five days. It is a moderate twining vine, easily kept in a hanging basket or trained up a short trellis, and tolerates brighter light and drier conditions than many understory Hoyas.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Hoya nicholsoniae
Steve's Leaves — Hoya nicholsoniae (white flower form)

planting.note: Grow as an upright tabletop plant that will cascade with age; native to limestone cliffs in full tropical sun, it tolerates brighter light than most Hoyas here but still flowers well in bright, filtered exposure indoors.

directions: Hoya cumingiana, native to limestone cliffs in the Philippines, Borneo, and Java, is a fast, hardy grower with small, scallop-edged leaves packed tightly along the stems on very short internodes, giving young plants a dense, bushy look before the stems lengthen and begin to cascade under their own weight. Its umbels of 10-15 yellow, star-shaped flowers are centered with a contrasting maroon corona, and the fragrance — strongest after dark — has been likened to ripe mango with a hint of cinnamon, unlike any other scent profile among the Hoyas in this dataset. Its naturally upright-then-trailing habit and tolerance for strong light make it a good choice for a sunny windowsill shelf rather than deep shade. Give it a support to climb if an upright form is preferred, or let it spill from a container.
sources: LiveTrends Design Group — Hoya cumingiana plant care

planting.note: Grow on a trellis or wire hoop in bright, filtered light; the long, wiry stems benefit from support and produce their best flower clusters once the vine is well established.

directions: Hoya elliptica, native to lowland forests of Thailand, Borneo, Malaysia, and Sumatra, earns its 'Turtle Shell' nickname from the raised, lighter-colored veins running across its fleshy, elliptical, olive-green leaves in a pattern reminiscent of a tortoise's carapace — a bolder relief than the finer venation of Hoya finlaysonii. Long, wiry stems carry dense, rounded umbels of roughly 25 flowers, each with a softly hairy white to near-white corolla and a glossy white corona marked with a dark pink center, blooming from spring into late summer with individual clusters lasting five to seven days. As an epiphyte in habitat, it appreciates a chunky, well-drained mix and a trellis or wire support for its wiry, climbing growth. Bright, filtered light produces the most reliable flowering.
sources: World of Succulents — Hoya elliptica (Turtle Shell Hoya)

Kew Plants of the World Online — Hoya elliptica

planting.note: Grow on a trellis in bright, filtered light with high heat and humidity; this Papua New Guinea epiphyte grows quickly once established and can bloom at any time of year rather than on a strict seasonal cycle.

directions: Hoya megalaster, an epiphyte from the primary forests of Papua New Guinea, takes its name (Greek for 'large star') from its dramatic dark purplish-pink, star-shaped flowers, which can reach nearly 2 inches across and open up to a dozen per umbel — a bolder, richer color than the pale pink or white blooms typical of most other Hoyas in this dataset. The shiny, dark-green, elliptical leaves are dimpled between lighter veins and emerge with a reddish flush on new growth, adding ornamental interest even between bloom cycles. Given ample heat, humidity, and bright filtered light, it is a fast, vigorous climber that can flower at any time of year rather than only in a fixed season. Provide a trellis for its slender climbing stems and keep the mix evenly moist but well-drained.
sources: World of Succulents — Hoya megalaster
Vermont Hoyas — Hoya megalaster
Hoya Store Australia — Hoya megalaster (IML 1080 H66)

planting.note: Grow as a slow-growing houseplant vine in bright indirect light with excellent drainage; a full stem cutting with at least one node is required to produce new growth, since single-leaf cuttings (as with the plain species) can root but will not branch.

directions: Hoya kerrii 'Albomarginata' is a variegated selection of the familiar Sweetheart Hoya, distinguished by a creamy yellow-to-white band edging each thick, heart-shaped leaf around a green center, creating a 'heart within a heart' pattern that the plain green species entirely lacks. Growth is noticeably slower than the standard green Hoya kerrii, a common trade-off with variegated Hoya cultivars, and mature vines eventually produce small, star-shaped, creamy-white flowers with rose-purple centers in summer. The thick, succulent leaves store water well, so the mix should dry out substantially between waterings. Bright indirect light is needed both to keep the cream variegation crisp and to bring the vine to flowering size.
sources: World of Succulents — Hoya kerrii f. albomarginata
Plantura — Hoya kerrii care guide
Patuxent Nursery — Hoya kerrii Albomarginata

planting.note: Grow in a hanging basket or trained up a small trellis in bright indirect light; stronger light intensifies the pink and cream variegation, while low light causes new leaves to revert toward plain green.

directions: Hoya australis 'Lisa' (also sold as 'Tricolor') is a variegated sport of the species grown for thick, waxy leaves splashed in cream, yellow, and multiple shades of green, with new growth emerging a vivid pink before settling into its mature marbled pattern — a far showier foliage display than the solid dark-green leaves of the standard Hoya australis. Its twining stems grow in an upright, self-winding habit, often coiling around neighboring stems as they lengthen, and mature plants produce the same fragrant, white, star-shaped flowers with pink centers as the species. Because variegated tissue photosynthesizes less efficiently, this cultivar grows more slowly than plain green Hoya australis and benefits from slightly brighter light to maintain both good color and steady growth. It shares the species' relative cold tolerance for a Hoya, though the variegated leaves are somewhat more cold-sensitive than solid green foliage.
sources: plantlust — Hoya australis 'Lisa' / 'Tricolor'
Vermont Hoyas — Hoya australis 'Lisa'
